chunks: Typical configurable GPIO settings. The question: What are some typical configurable GPIO settings?
A GPIO pin has a small set of settings, and every microcontroller family has the same set under different names. They fall into groups.
What the pin is: input, output, analog, or handed to a peripheral. How it drives: output type, starting value, edge speed and strength.
How it senses: pull resistors, input filtering, and interrupts.
Picture a faucet with several dials. One dial chooses which appliance the pipe feeds. Another sets how hard the water can flow. A third sets how quickly you open the valve.
If you slam a valve open, the pipes bang and shake the whole house. The same happens on a chip: a very fast edge on one pin creates noise on the supply and in the air.
The settings fall into four groups. Whenever you meet an unfamiliar MCU, find where each group's registers live; the details differ but the groups do not.
Mode: whether the pin is a digital input, a digital output, an analog input, or handed to a peripheral (a built-in hardware block).
Alternate function: routing a peripheral's signal, such as UART TX or SPI clock, to the pin instead of the GPIO block. Output type: push-pull or open-drain.
Slew rate (speed): how fast the output switches between low and high (each switch is an edge). Slower edges cause less noise.
Drive strength: how much current the pin is allowed to deliver. Stronger drive makes sharper current spikes.
Interrupt: a pin-change event that makes the processor stop and respond, chosen as rising edge, falling edge or both.
Set up three pins. An SPI clock running at 40 megahertz is an alternate function, push-pull, with high speed so its edges stay clean.
An LED enable is a plain output, push-pull, at the lowest speed. An I2C data line is an alternate function, open-drain, with an external pull-up.
A 2 nanoseconds edge makes noise up to roughly 160 megahertz, while a 10 nanoseconds edge reaches only about 32 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"I think of three groups. What the pin is: mode (input, output, alternate function, analog) and which alternate function.
How it drives: output type, push-pull or open-drain, initial value, drive strength and slew rate, which trade edge speed against EMI and ground bounce.
How it senses: pull-up, pull-down or none, Schmitt trigger or filter, and interrupt edge, enable and wake-up.
Plus housekeeping: atomic set/reset registers, a lock bit, and remember most pins reset to floating inputs."
